extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of theology, philosophy, and literary criticism (readers of Coleridge/Christian apologetics)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for judging religious doctrines and philosophical systems with respect to evidence, practical effect, and relation to Christian faith; emphasizes interplay of internal (spiritual/ideal) and external (historical) evidence and the proper use of reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish internal (spiritual/ideal) and external (historical) evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: External testimony (outward evidence) applies to outward events and appearances; internal evidence (ideas within us, moral sense, spiritual perception) is the sole sufficient evidence for spiritual truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External evidence may excite and evolve internal ideas and can support the historical reality of events, but it cannot by itself constitute an article of religion; the spiritual recognition that constitutes saving faith is from within. Treat outward testimony as subsidiary to internal spiritual testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threefold criterion for admitting an article of faith
rubrics_metrics.description: In each article of faith conviction is determined (1) intuitively on its logical possibility, (2) discursively on its analogy to doctrines already believed, and (3) historically on the degree of evidence a posteriori.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three factors interdepend: logical (a priori) conditions the others; analogy and historical evidence are influenced by it. The required historical evidence is inversely related to the strength of the a priori and analogical reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not substitute historical proof for internal evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a mistake to attempt to establish all religious doctrine by outward/historical evidence alone, while neglecting the inward spiritual evidence necessary to give the outward facts their religious significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the 'Antiquarian theory of faith' which seeks to make historical attestation the sole foundation; without the internal ideas, external evidence is empty and unmeaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'rationalism' (misplaced use of reason) in spiritual matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Rationalism is the undue employment of reason in religion — asking for reasons 'out of place' or demanding positive logical proof of spiritual verities that belong to the province of the spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize limits of speculative/theoretical reason: asking for purely discursive proof of matters properly judged by the spiritual faculties is a category error. Yet reason can show impossibility of disproof and has a role without being sole arbiter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give primacy to the spiritual/moral faculties in judging religion
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral sense and inner spiritual perception are central to recognizing religious truth; reason and outward evidence should be used to clarify and support, but the spirit within must be able to see the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate the 'spiritual mind' that perceives internal correspondences, safeguards against mere reliance on external attestation, and discerns the internal coherence and moral power of doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge doctrines by their practical application and moral efficacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious doctrine should be tested by its capacity for practical application, relation to appointed ends, and its tendency to moral improvement; speculative precision alone is inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of critics who handle sacred themes with technical precision but ignore moral tendencies and effects. The speculative mind is ill-qualified to judge purely by abstract logical niceties without reference to practical outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize metaphorical/scriptural language without denying real substance
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between denying a literal formulation of metaphors used in Scripture and denying the reality they signify; saying metaphors are not to be taken literally is not equivalent to denying the causal or saving act they represent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid imputing heterodoxy to writers who view biblical descriptions as figurative; accept that transcendent acts may be known by their effects and consequences without rigid literal definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analytic philosophy to clarify religion rather than replace it
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical or analytic philosophy (as exemplified by Kant) can clarify the intellectual form of religion and render its coherence more evident, but it should not be adopted as a substitute for Christianity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open to non-religious analytic insights that free thought from irrational doctrines and help show correspondence between revelation and human reason, while avoiding making the philosophy itself the entire basis of faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of partial or truncated argumentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting only part of a reasoning or cutting a doctrine 'in half' may render it false or injurious by omission; treatises adapted for certain audiences must avoid leaving out essential inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that arguments are shown in full, especially where complex philosophical or theological inferences are at stake; partial presentations can be misunderstood and misapplied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixing inconsistent systems or using 'fine sayings' as confutations
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics sometimes take eloquent phrases or superficial remarks as definitive confutations of opponents' views, or mix inconsistent elements from different schools without regard to coherence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not substitute rhetorical flourish for rigorous refutation; assess systems for internal consistency and beware of partisan judges slightly acquainted with the writings they condemn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginative power as a criterion for reconstruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Imaginative power — the ability to 'bring the many into one' and judge by reference to the whole — is essential for reconstruction and sympathetic synthesis of ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate thinkers and critics for the presence of imaginative integrative capacity; a lack of imaginative power leads to atomized, purely analytic judgments that miss overarching unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical evidence's probative value depends on intrinsic probability
rubrics_metrics.description: The probability of an event is part of its historic evidence; a fact probable in itself may be believed on less historical testimony, while improbable facts require stronger historical attestation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing historical claims, weigh intrinsic plausibility (logical/analogical grounds) against documentary/historical testimony; stronger a priori reasons reduce the burden of historical proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious inquiry should not despise subtle analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who value correctness and clarity should not despise the labors of subtle analysts; clearing and correcting intellectual form can be beneficial to religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance respect for spiritual sensibility with appreciation for analytic work that clarifies doctrine; allow critical analysis to reveal limits and structure of human understanding without assuming hostility to faith.
